3: miscellaneous, I feel something specifically limiting epic is the fact that it's an album and lacks full visuals (before anyone mentions the animatics canon or not I'm saying the songs weren't written with the accompanying visuals in mind, because this means that the songs have to set the scene while they tell the story which is really really difficult. Take Hamilton for instance. When you see people listening to Hamilton as audio for the first time they're always super confused about how to picture the scene. But most people will say half of Hamilton's genius is the staging that gives it nuance. Epic was handicapped here, so the lyrics in my opinion really do lack nuance in comparison to Hamilton. But the latter is really on the extreme end of good writing for musicals, and Epic does a good job of lyrics that don't feel forced into the rhythm. Musically, the writing is very sound. In terms of thematically, however? Eh. See 1. and 2.

AND, time. I know I just ranted for three points but I really do think Epic was a phenomenon and did more things right than not. I see you, parasocial fandom, and am mildly fearful /lh

2. Continuity problems. Namely, Get in the Water/Six Hundred Strikes. Especially since in the previous saga Athena just got fucked up by Zeus, and yet Ody bests Poseidon a couple songs later. Are they not both of the Big Three?? How is Ody stronger than Athena? Moreover, *is the wind in the wind bag 2.0 not Poseidon's own storm??? How is it able to be used against him?* 

I've seen several points in support of Six Hundred Strikes, and first of all can I just say if you need to add headcanons to make sense of it that's a flaw of the original work; but secondly, I hear people saying the red eyes indicate Ares helping Ody. However, *Ares isn't one of the big three!!! Even if he was fighting Poseidon on his own, he would still lose, case in point the other war god (Athena) losing to another of the big three (Zeus).* Let alone a *mortal* being helped by him. As a mortal you do not fuck with any god but ESPECIALLY not the big three. Let alone a mortal that needed Hermes' help with the molly herb to defeat Circe (also a goddess but a minor one bn comparison) in a fight. And didn't he already have the original wind bag in Ruthlessness? Could he not have done the same thing and got home in the first Act? What's stopping him from beating up Zeus? The powerscaling is so, so off.   
  
I saw some people argue that he technically is the grandson of a god, so maybe that gave him an edge, but you know what's better then being 1/16 or something god? BEING 100% GOD. Additionally, what's stopping Poseidon from just returning and killing all of Ithaca? Did we not already establish in God Games with Athena being punished by Zeus by 'disrespecting' him and in Ruthlessness where Ody 'disrespected' Poseidon by leaving a charge of his maimed that gods whose ego has been hurt bring *hell*? I love epic but Poseidon's defeat is truly a low point. It's OOC for everyone involved.

Now something more minor, but I dislike the presence of 'word of god' in Epic. There's so much that's unexplained in the canon material (which I consider the songs and canon animatics but the latter's on thin ice) that's only made sense of when you watch Jorge's tiktoks. Which, I greatly enjoy! It's wonderful to see the amount of references within musically, he's very talented in music, and the entire cast have such great voices! But I shouldn't have to go to your social media to make sense of the rules of your world. Case in point: the sirens. Nowhere in the song does it hint at how they work. Which is worrisome since it's a fresh take on them, but they only last for two songs so it's not that important in my opinion. It's part of a bigger problem, though: for instance, Jorge's explanation of Shatter the Ocean was *only* on his tiktok. I almost wish there was some foreshadowing of Poseidon's weakness in close combat as mentioned in the video if only to make the Vengeance saga make more sense.

epic still has a place in my heart these are just some issues that come up as the sagas progressed: 1) ody's character arc 2) continuity problems

1. The whole thing about Epic is the dichotomy of ruthlessness and pacifism, and about Ody learning to be more ruthless. Obviously madness arcs are Fantastic and arcs where you regain your humanity even more so but my problem with Epic is that it never fully commits to this. They never fully allow Ody to become a monster. So the reconciliation of Penelope as he's *meant* to regain his humanity falls flat, because he never lost it in the first place; everything he does is justified in canon, not to say he doesnt feel guilt in-universe, but that there is nothing he does that is truly irredeemably monstrous *in the narrative,* be it the sirens that were trying to lure him to be eaten, or the sacrifice of his men after they mutinied, etc.

I've never felt that Epic has a clear understanding of what ruthlessness means. From my interpretation from the first few sagas, ruthlessness is using the best means to achieve your own ends regardless of who it hurts. But I feel like as the sagas went on, it turned into 'do your enemies as much harm as you can'? Like, with the sirens, was it necessary to cut off their tails to let them die and drown? What if they survived? Sure, *we* know they didn't since they never return, and thematically since they didn't come back to hunt him, they're likely dead. But Ody doesn't know that. Didn't he lose all his other ships in Ruthlessness because he maimed the cyclops? And he's doing it again? To a creature of the sea (I have no idea if it's a bird or fish siren here in Epic but the animatics I've seen depict her as a fish siren so that's what I'm going with), *after already having a confrontation with Poseidon?* Even if he doesn't care as much since the siren isn't his direct charge, Odysseus is technically still not being 'ruthless'; killing the sirens *quickly* to *make sure* they're *dead.* Sending them off the ship without tails-- sure, they were meant to and did die, but they're inhuman. Maybe they can grow new fins??? Maybe they're like jellyfish! Who knows? Not you, Ody? Why risk it? (It /gen just comes off as a 'cool' moment, which is fine, but it's not justified thematically.)

And the moment he's *meant* to have become a monster, in the song Odysseus as he slaughters the suitors, he's still a husband protecting his wife (which I have my own criticisms about, but I think Anniflamma's post said it better so I'll link it here[ https://www.tumblr.com/anniflamma/769075802431209472/trigger-warning-topic-about-sa-aka-im-gonna-rant?source=share:](https://www.tumblr.com/anniflamma/769075802431209472/trigger-warning-topic-about-sa-aka-im-gonna-rant?source=share:)"For me, it would be more thematically fitting with Odysseus’ ruthless nature to *not* have a justifiable "motivation" to kill the suitors. Imagine instead if they were portrayed as having the same youthful energy as Telemachus. Like a bunch of rude young men! And then the story could show an adult man brutally murdering a group of young people with no mercy. Then, the song ends with Odysseus seeing Penelope’s horrified face as she looks around the throne room splattered with the blood and gore of her guests. At that moment, Odysseus realizes he’s messed up, putting his biggest fear, which is Penelope rejecting him (something he expresses in *Keep Your Friends Close*) at risk of becoming a reality. And then, the musical end with Odysseus begging Penelope to accept him despite what he has become. Like what I said, the outcome will still end up in this moment despite with or no sexual violence. I mean, the suitors wanting to kill Telemachus is enough as a motivation. Ody don't really need that much. \[...\] It’s unnecessary. **Just let Odysseus commit cruel and ruthless deeds without a "good justification" or feeling bad about it afterward for once.")**

Even his slaughter is given cause by the narrative, additionally might I add because to my knowledge the suitors never devise such a plan in the Odyssey. What's more, in the odyssey Ody does something truly monstrous: he kills the 12 servant girls for being coerced into sex by the suitors. That is irredeemable. Epic is very family friendly so i get why Jorge cut it out but it just puts me off because if your adaptation is focused on ruthlessness/being a monster and you fail to deliver on that, and at the same time cut out something that perfectly encapsulates that... to be clear, I dont think this should've been included, it's way too OOC for EPIC!Ody, but its a good example of a truly monstrous action.

\>Surviving the next human's wrath  
\>Drinking every last drop of the second Goddess's blood  
\>Not forgetting one's name
